results.prompt: A desk for planning my sister's 30th birthday party.

verdict.reason: The desk is specific to a 30th birthday party and well configured: tables have sensible columns and select options, pages have real starter content, and the fields, sticky and calculator are relevant. Minor flaws: the task tracker and shopping list tables are suggested with no rows, and the cost-per-guest calculator is a generic widget, so it is unclear how it links to the budget or headcount fields. The three webviews are also somewhat filler, and Pinterest and Spotify may not embed.

data.intent: Get fully prepared for a fintech job interview next week: research the company, rehearse stories and questions, track the interview rounds, and keep key logistics and references in view.

suggestions.title: 7-day interview prep plan
suggestions.reason: A day-by-day roadmap so the week before the interview is structured, not frantic

content.text: Interview Prep Plan
Goal: walk in knowing the company, the role, and my 5-6 strongest stories cold. Work backwards from interview day.
Days 7-5: Research and foundations
Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Complete the company research brief
Map my experience to each requirement
Draft my 'Tell me about yourself' pitch
Days 4-3: Stories and technical depth
Write 6 STAR stories in the story bank
Review the fintech concepts cheat sheet
Do 2 timed technical or case practice sessions
Days 2-1: Rehearse and logistics
Do a full mock interview out loud (record it)
Finalize 5 questions to ask the interviewers
Test video link, audio, and camera, or plan the route
Lay out outfit and print or open a copy of my resume
Interview day
Light review only. Skim the story bank, eat well, arrive 10 minutes early, and send thank-you notes within 24 hours.

suggestions.title: Company research brief
suggestions.reason: One place to capture what the company does, how it makes money, and where it's headed

content.text: Company Research Brief
What they do
One-sentence product description, target customers (consumers, SMBs, banks, enterprises), and core value proposition.
Business model
Revenue streams: interchange, subscription, interest/lending, SaaS fees, take rate?
Funding stage, latest round, key investors, or public ticker
Key partners (sponsor banks, card networks, processors)
Competitors and positioning
List 3 direct competitors and how this company differentiates (pricing, UX, compliance, distribution, tech).
Regulation and risk
Licenses held (money transmitter, banking-as-a-service, broker-dealer), compliance obligations (KYC/AML, PCI DSS, SOC 2), and any recent regulatory news.
Recent news and milestones
Latest product launch or announcement
Latest funding, earnings, or leadership change
Why this company, why me
Two or three genuine reasons I'm excited about their mission, plus how my background solves a problem they have right now.

suggestions.reason: Refresh the domain vocabulary interviewers expect you to speak fluently

content.text: Fintech Concepts Cheat Sheet
Payments
Payment lifecycle: authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, and chargebacks/disputes
Players: issuer, acquirer, card network, processor, payment gateway
Rails: ACH, wire, RTP/FedNow, SEPA, card networks
Compliance and risk
KYC / KYB, AML transaction monitoring, sanctions screening (OFAC)
PCI DSS, SOC 2, GDPR/CCPA data handling
Fraud signals: velocity checks, device fingerprinting, risk scoring
Engineering and data themes
Idempotency keys and exactly-once processing for money movement
Double-entry ledgers and reconciliation
Eventual consistency, audit trails, and observability for financial systems
Business metrics
TPV (total payment volume), take rate, net revenue retention, CAC/LTV, default and loss rates, unit economics per transaction.
Terms I still need to look up
Add unfamiliar terms from the job description here

suggestions.title: 'Tell me about yourself' pitch
suggestions.reason: A tight 90-second opener you can rehearse until it's automatic
suggestions.content:
# Tell me about yourself (90 sec)

**Present:** I'm currently a [role] at [company], where I [biggest responsibility and one measurable result].

**Past:** Before that, I [1-2 experiences that built the skills this role needs], including [specific achievement with a number].

**Future:** I'm excited about [company] because [specific product/mission reason], and I want to bring my experience in [skill] to help [team goal from the job description].

---

**Rules:** keep it under 90 seconds, end on why this company, and never recite the resume line by line.

suggestions.title: Questions to ask the interviewers
suggestions.reason: Thoughtful questions signal seriousness and help you evaluate the company

content.text: Questions to Ask
About the role
What would success look like in the first 90 days?
What is the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?
About the business
How is regulation shaping your roadmap over the next year?
Where do you see the biggest competitive threat, and how are you responding?
About the team and culture
How do the team and the compliance/risk functions work together on launches?
What do you enjoy most about working here?
Closing
What are the next steps and timeline? Is there anything about my background you'd like me to clarify?

Goal
Drive awareness and qualified demo requests for the product launch on 14 November 2026 through a six-week content campaign (19 Oct to 29 Nov), with the launch landing in week 4.
Audience
Decision-makers and hands-on evaluators at B2B companies who feel the pain our product solves. Primary: team leads and ops managers. Secondary: finance and IT approvers.

The problem we solve, in one sentence the buyer would say themselves
Proof: demo video, early customer results, clear differentiators
Call to action: book a demo or start a trial
Success metrics
Agree demo-request target and log it in the Demo target field
Agree weekly reporting metrics: impressions, clicks, signups, demos booked

Risks
The launch date already moved once because the payments review slipped. Keep pre-launch content evergreen so another slip does not force rework.

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

Our team wiki currently lives in [current wiki tool]. This project moves it into PlexiiWrite so the team has one place to find, write and maintain shared knowledge. This brief sets out what we want from the move, what is and is not included, how the work will unfold, and what could go wrong.
Goals
The move should leave us with a wiki that is easier to use than the one we have now, not just a copy of it in a new home. Specifically, we want to:
Move all content we still need into PlexiiWrite with its structure, links and ownership intact.
Retire the old wiki so there is a single source of truth and no one wonders which version is current.
Use the move as a chance to archive outdated pages instead of carrying them over.
Have the team working in PlexiiWrite day to day by the cutover date, with no gap in access to information.
Success means the old wiki is read-only or shut down by [target date], every active page has a home in PlexiiWrite, and the team can find what they need without asking where it went.
Scope

In scope are all pages, attachments and embedded media in the current wiki, the page hierarchy, internal links, and access permissions. Also in scope are a short content audit before migration, basic guidance for the team on writing and organizing pages in PlexiiWrite, and a decision on what happens to the old wiki afterward.

Out of scope are rewriting content that is still accurate, redesigning the information architecture beyond what the audit shows is necessary, and migrating tools or documents that live outside the wiki. Anything we want to add later goes on a follow-up list rather than into this project.
Timeline
The work runs in five phases. Durations and dates are to be confirmed once the owner has reviewed the size of the wiki.
Audit and planning, [dates]: inventory the pages, decide what to archive, and map the new structure and permissions.
Test migration, [dates]: move a representative sample, check formatting, links and attachments, and fix the process.
Full migration, [dates]: move the remaining content and review it with page owners.
Cutover, [date]: freeze the old wiki, announce the switch and point everyone to PlexiiWrite.
Follow-up, [dates]: fix broken links, gather feedback and decide when to decommission the old wiki.
Risks
Formatting, tables or embedded content may not transfer cleanly. The test migration is meant to surface this early, and we should budget time for manual cleanup.
Internal links may break when pages move. We should check links after migration and keep the old wiki readable for a short period.
Permissions may not map one to one. Review access for sensitive pages before cutover, not after.
People may keep editing the old wiki out of habit, which splits the content. A clear freeze date and a visible announcement reduce this.
Page owners may be too busy to review their content. Name the owners early and give them a firm review window.
The audit may show more content than expected, which would push the timeline. Agree now who can approve a change to the dates.
Ownership
The project owner is [owner name], with [page reviewers or team leads] responsible for checking their sections. Questions and decisions during the migration go to [owner name].

content.text: Welcome

Welcome to the team. This guide covers what your first week looks like, the tools you will use every day, and how we handle escalations. You are not expected to know everything by Friday. The goal of week one is that you can handle straightforward conversations confidently, know where to find answers, and know exactly when and how to ask for help.
Your onboarding buddy is [buddy name] and your team lead is [team lead name]. If you are unsure about anything in this guide, ask either of them. Questions in week one are expected and welcome.
What good support looks like here

Our job is to resolve the customer's problem, not just close the ticket. A good reply is accurate, clear, and written for the person who will read it, who is usually busy and often frustrated. A few habits will carry you a long way:
Read the whole ticket and any prior history before you reply.
Answer the question the customer actually asked, then anticipate the obvious next one.
Be honest about what you do not know. "I'm checking this and will update you by [time]" is better than a guess.
Never promise a fix, refund, date, or feature unless you have confirmed it is possible.
Leave a clear internal note on every ticket so the next person can pick it up without starting over.
Your first week
Treat the following as a suggested pace. Your team lead will adjust it to fit your schedule and the current workload.
Day one: access and orientation

Your goal is to get set up and to understand the shape of the team. Confirm you can log in to every tool listed below, introduce yourself in [team chat channel], and meet your buddy. Spend the rest of the day reading our product documentation as a customer would, then read through a sample of recently resolved tickets to see how replies are written.
Days two and three: learn the product and shadow

Work through the product by actually using it. Set up a test account, follow the main customer journeys, and note where you get confused, since customers will get confused in the same places. Sit in on live conversations with your buddy, or read their tickets in real time. Ask why they chose a particular answer or macro. By the end of day three you should be able to explain our core product to someone who has never seen it.
Day four: handle tickets with a safety net

Start answering real tickets, beginning with the simpler categories. Your buddy or team lead will review your replies before they are sent, or shortly after. Expect feedback on tone, accuracy, and internal notes. This is normal and is how everyone improves.
Day five: review and reflect

Sit down with your team lead to go over what went well, where you felt stuck, and what to focus on in week two. Bring a list of the questions you still have. Together you will agree on the ticket types you can handle on your own and the ones that still need a second pair of eyes.
Tools
You will work across a small set of tools. Your team lead will confirm your access to each of them on day one.
[Helpdesk tool] is where all customer conversations live. You will use it to reply, add internal notes, tag tickets, and track status.
[Knowledge base] holds our help articles and internal answers. Search here before asking, and flag anything that is wrong or out of date.
[Team chat tool] is for quick questions, handoffs, and incident updates. Use the right channel, and keep customer-specific details out of public channels.
[Admin or account lookup tool] lets you view customer accounts and settings. Only access an account when you have a support reason to do so.
[Bug or issue tracker] is where confirmed product problems are logged and followed. Search it before filing anything new.

Customer data is sensitive. Only access what you need to resolve the ticket, never share account details with anyone who has not been verified, and follow [link to security and privacy policy] at all times.
How we handle escalations

An escalation means passing a ticket to someone with more access, authority, or expertise than you have. Escalating is a normal part of the job, not a sign that you failed. What matters is that you escalate at the right time, with the right information, and that the customer is never left wondering what is happening.
When to escalate
Escalate when any of the following applies:
You have a likely product bug or outage that is not already logged.
The issue needs a technical investigation beyond your access or training.
The customer is asking for something outside your authority, such as an exception, a refund above your limit, or a policy decision.
The situation involves a security concern, a legal or privacy request, or a threat to leave a public review or take legal action.
The customer is distressed or the conversation has become hostile, and you are not confident a further reply will help.
You have worked the problem and are stuck. If you have spent more than [time threshold] without progress, ask for help.
If you are unsure whether something qualifies, ask in [escalation or help channel]. It is always better to ask early.
How to escalate
Before you pass a ticket on, make it easy for the next person to act without going back to the customer. Your escalation note should include:
A one or two line summary of the problem and its impact on the customer.
The customer's account or ID and the plan or tier they are on.
Exact steps to reproduce the issue, with screenshots or error messages where you have them.
What you have already tried and what the result was.
What you need from the person you are escalating to, and how urgent it is.

Then escalate through [escalation route, for example a ticket assignment, a form, or a channel], and tag the ticket with [escalation tag]. For urgent issues such as outages or security concerns, follow the urgent path in [link to incident or urgent escalation process] and contact [on-call or urgent contact].
Keeping the customer informed

Escalating does not end your responsibility to the customer. Tell them honestly that you are bringing in a colleague or specialist, what will happen next, and when they can expect an update. Do not promise a resolution time that you do not control. If the target response time for the escalated team is [target response time], share that as an expectation rather than a guarantee. Then check back on the ticket and update the customer at the time you committed to, even if the update is that you are still working on it.
After the escalation

When the escalated team responds, read what they did and why. Next time you see a similar issue, you may be able to resolve it yourself or write a stronger escalation. If you notice a gap in our documentation or macros, tell your team lead or update the knowledge base directly if you have permission.
Who to ask

For day-to-day questions, start with your buddy, [buddy name]. For workload, schedule, or performance questions, speak to your team lead, [team lead name]. For access problems, contact [IT or access contact]. For anything involving a security or privacy concern, go straight to [security contact] and your team lead.
End of week one checklist
By the end of your first week you should be able to say yes to each of these:
I can log in to every tool and know what each one is for.
I have used the product myself and can explain its main features.
I have answered real tickets and received feedback on them.
I know when to escalate, how to write a good escalation note, and where to send it.
I know who to go to for help with different kinds of questions.
I have talked through my first week with my team lead and agreed on my focus for week two.
If any of these are not true yet, that is fine. Tell your team lead so you can close the gap together.

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. This session is about a small skill with a big payoff: writing bug reports that get understood and fixed quickly. By the end, you should be able to write one that an engineer can act on without a single follow-up question.

slides.title: Why a good report matters
bullets: Engineers can only fix what they can understand
Missing details cause back-and-forth and delay
A clear report helps with triage and prioritization
Vague reports often get closed as not reproducible
Your time writing it saves everyone else's time reading it
slides.notes: Start with the cost of a bad report. Every question the engineer has to ask adds a day of waiting, and some bugs are lost entirely because nobody could reproduce them. A few minutes of care up front pays back many times over.

slides.title: The anatomy of a good report
bullets: A short, specific title that names the problem
Steps to reproduce, numbered and in order
Expected result versus actual result
Environment: device, OS, browser, app version
Evidence such as screenshots, recordings or logs
Severity and who is affected, if you know
slides.notes: Walk through each part and say why it is there. The title helps people scan a list, the steps let someone see the bug for themselves, and the expected versus actual contrast shows exactly what is wrong. Environment and evidence remove guesswork.

slides.title: Titles and steps that work
bullets: Weak title: "Checkout broken"
Better title: "Checkout button does nothing after applying a discount code"
One action per step, written so a newcomer could follow it
Start from a known state, such as logged out or an empty cart
Note whether it happens every time or only sometimes
slides.notes: Contrast the weak and better titles out loud. Then explain that steps should start from a clear starting point and use one action each. Mention that frequency matters: a bug that happens every time and one that happens occasionally are investigated very differently.

slides.title: Before you hit submit
bullets: Try to reproduce it a second time
Search for an existing report of the same issue
Report one problem per ticket
Stick to facts and leave out blame or guesses about the cause
Reread it as if you knew nothing about the situation
slides.notes: This is the quick checklist for the moment before submitting. Reproducing it once more catches flukes, and searching first avoids duplicates. Keep the tone neutral: describe what you saw, and leave theories about the cause to a short, clearly labeled note at the end if you have one.

slides.title: Putting it into practice
bullets: Use the same structure every time
Pick one recent bug and rewrite its report using today's anatomy
Ask a teammate to try following your steps
Share questions or template ideas in [team channel or owner name]
slides.notes: Close by making it practical. Ask everyone to take one bug they have seen recently and rewrite the report using the structure we covered. If a teammate can follow your steps and see the same problem, the report is good.

Refund policy FAQ

Can I get a refund if I change my mind?

Yes. If you ask within 30 days of your purchase, we will refund you in full.

What happens after the 30 days are up?

Once the 30-day window has passed, we do not offer refunds on monthly plans. You can cancel at any time to stop future charges.

Does the policy work differently for annual plans?

Yes. Annual plans are refunded pro rata. Instead of an all-or-nothing decision, you get back the portion of the plan you have paid for but not used.

What does pro rata mean in practice?

We take the price of your annual plan and subtract the value of the time you have already had. The remainder is the amount we refund. The sooner you cancel, the larger the refund.

How do I request a refund?

Contact our support team at [support email] and include the email address on your account. We will confirm the refund amount with you before we process it.

Still have a question?

Write to us at [support email] and we will be happy to help.
